supplement.where: SI Appendix, cited throughout but neither appended nor embedded in the saved PDF; no separate appendix URL is supplied. The paper links preregistrations, surveys, raw data and reproducible R code at https://osf.io/pdjwh/?view_only=d4d76b6c6e9343e99bcc146a68fbd578 (PDF pp. 11-12, Materials and Methods). The finalizer could not retrieve the supplement: urllib requests to the OSF API, OSF project and alternate SSRN page all failed with WinError 10013.
supplement.holds: Contents described by the main text, not independently inspected: Table S1 is cited for contemporaneous playoff betting odds (p. 5) and data-collection and sport-outcome dates (p. 12); Table S2 for numbers preregistered, dropout rates and final sample sizes across experiments (p. 12); Table S3 for knowledge-screen questions (p. 12); Table S4 for no-LLM participants excluded for using an LLM (p. 5); Section 3 for accuracy, confidence and calibration details (p. 5), and Table S5 for percent confidence (p. 8); Section 4 for robustness checks restoring excluded participants, splitting no-LLM participants by search-engine use, controlling gender and using team standings as the accuracy benchmark (pp. 9-10); Table S12 for percentile benchmarking, Tables S13-S16 for quartile analyses, Table S21 for crowd-level unique-team comparisons, and Section 5 for the ancillary occupation-guessing experiment (p. 11). The PDF does not establish that Table S2 contains actual randomized totals or individual-arm counts. Exact hit-rate statistics, crowd-level numerical results and their uncertainty are absent from the saved PDF; their availability in the cited appendix remains unverified.

paper_design_summary: Four online experiments (Prolific and MTurk; 396, 213, 803 and 400 people analyzed) randomly assigned individuals to list the MLB or NFL teams they expected to make the playoffs, either with an LLM (Perplexity AI or Google Bard, own prompts) or with their own judgment and a browser or search engine. Experiment 3 crossed LLM use with a 10-cent bonus per correct team, and Experiment 4 crossed LLM use in a first and a second listing stage. Each person's list was scored for the number of unique teams and the number and share classed as accurate using contemporaneous betting odds; the paper also reports no difference in crowd-level unique-team counts and refers to the uninspected SI Table S21 for details (PDF pp. 4-8, 11-13).

participants.exclusions: Preregistered analysis criteria: all knowledge questions answered correctly, at least one team named, and no LLM use unless assigned to the LLM condition (PDF p. 12). Naming no team and self-reported LLM use are assessed after the task; the latter exclusion applies to the no-LLM arm (p. 5), so the analysis is not intention-to-treat. The PDF gives no exact exclusion count, randomized total or per-arm analyzed counts. Table S2 is described as a summary of numbers preregistered, dropout rates and final sample sizes (p. 12); Table S4 is cited for excluded no-LLM participants who used an LLM (p. 5). Those tables were not inspected, and their coverage of actual randomized and per-arm counts is unknown. The paper reports 396 people analyzed after screenings (p. 12).

outcomes.name: Number of hypotheses generated (unique teams listed)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of unique teams in each participant's list. Robustness checks (no exclusions, no-LLM participants split by search-engine use, gender covariate) in SI Section 4.

contrasts.reported: M LLM = 8.72, SD = 3.76 vs. M no-LLM = 5.99, SD = 3.56; t(394) = 7.41, p < .001, d = 0.745 (per-arm n not printed; total N = 396)
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Results, Experiments 1-2; p. 6, Fig. 1 panel A

outcomes.name: Number of accurate hypotheses (accuracy based on contemporaneous playoff betting odds)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of listed teams that were accurate against playoff betting odds at the time of the experiment (SI Table S1); team standings as an alternative benchmark in SI Section 4. Exploratory analysis. The main text does not state the decision rule that converts betting odds into accurate versus inaccurate hypotheses (PDF p. 5; SI Table S1 cited but not inspected).

contrasts.reported: M LLM = 5.82, SD = 2.42 vs. M no-LLM = 4.29, SD = 2.92; t(380.75) = 5.70, p < .001, d = 0.573 (per-arm n not printed)

outcomes.name: Percent accuracy (actual hit rate: accurate hypotheses divided by all hypotheses)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Participant-level percent accuracy: number of correct hypotheses divided by the total number generated (PDF p. 8, accuracy definition; Fig. 4(b), p. 9). This is a proportion derived from two counts, not a raw count. The current codebook defines category_count as counts and provides no explicit label for an accuracy proportion, so measure is null pending an internal coding convention. Output scoring, participant unit and the stated formula are confirmed. SI Section 3 is cited for details (p. 5), but was not inspected; exact per-experiment hit-rate statistics are not printed in this PDF.

contrasts.reported: Text, pooled over the four experiments: LLM use resulted 'in a similar percentage of accurate hypotheses (i.e., actual hit rate) as when an LLM was not used.' Fig. 4(b) plots means with 95% CIs only; the Exp 1 LLM point lies slightly below the no-LLM point and the intervals overlap. No per-experiment test in this PDF.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, 'LLMs do not reduce accuracy but do reduce confidence in hypotheses'; p. 9, Fig. 4(b)

eligibility.reason: Random assignment is explicit: Qualtrics administered random condition assignment (PDF p. 11, Materials and Methods), with individual assignment to the two LLM/no-LLM arms in Experiments 1-2 and four factorial cells in Experiments 3-4 (pp. 12-13). The four experiments analyzed 396, 213, 803 and 400 people after screenings, respectively (pp. 12-13); each independently exceeds 50. Actual randomized totals and individual-arm analyzed counts are not printed, and the PDF does not establish that the uninspected SI Table S2 supplies them. The main outcomes are objectively scored on the output participants produced: unique teams per person (p. 5), accurate-hypothesis counts and proportions (pp. 5-8), and unique teams across the crowd in each condition (p. 11). The unresolved point is scope, not whether scoring occurred. The task enumerates a finite set of sports-playoff forecasts (p. 4, Paradigm), judged by quantity and accuracy rather than novelty, originality or creativity. Codebook sections 1 and 3 do not explicitly settle whether these forecasts, including their crowd-level breadth, qualify as creative ideation or homogenization evidence. As in the reconciled form, this scope question is carried under criterion 3 rather than counted again under criterion 1. Core therefore remains unclear pending an internal scope decision; no additional source is needed to describe the main task. The ancillary occupation-guessing experiment cannot independently establish eligibility because its specific design, sample size, scoring method and timing are not given in the saved PDF (p. 11; SI Section 5 uninspected). The abstract total of 1,814 (p. 2) conflicts with the sum of the explicit analyzed study counts, 1,812; that discrepancy does not affect the per-study threshold.

one_line_finding: In four online experiments analyzing 396, 213, 803 and 400 people (PDF pp. 12-13), LLM assistance increased the number of playoff teams listed (Experiment 1: 8.72 vs 5.99, d = 0.745; Experiment 2: 8.43 vs 5.42, d = 0.676, p. 5; Experiment 4 pooled: 7.50 vs 6.07, d = 0.356, p. 7), the Experiment 3 incentive attenuated the gap (8.76 vs 6.56 without incentives; 9.87 vs 9.22 with incentives, p = .306, p. 6), and the authors report similar hit rates (p. 8) and no crowd-level unique-team difference (p. 11, referring to uninspected SI Table S21).
open_questions: Scope remains unresolved for criterion 3: does enumerating a finite set of sports-playoff forecasts, scored by quantity and betting-odds accuracy, qualify as creative ideation, or does the crowd-level unique-team comparison qualify as homogenization evidence? The task and outcome methods are adequately described in PDF pp. 4-5, 8 and 11. This requires an internal Review 1 scope decision, not another source.

Figure 4 grouping for Experiment 3 is unresolved: the caption excludes incentivized cells (PDF p. 9; repeated p. 17), but its total-hypothesis points do not align with the printed unincentivized cell means (p. 6). No values are extracted from unlabelled dot positions. Posted analysis data/code or author clarification are needed to establish the plotted cells; this does not affect the assignment or participant threshold.

The abstract prints total N = 1,814 (PDF p. 2), whereas the analyzed counts 396, 213, 803 and 400 (pp. 12-13) sum to 1,812. The source does not explain the discrepancy; author clarification is needed, but each stated study count exceeds 50.

Actual randomized totals, exact exclusion counts and individual-arm analyzed counts are absent from the saved PDF. Table S2 is described only as covering numbers preregistered, dropout rates and final sample sizes (PDF p. 12), and Table S4 is cited for no-LLM participants excluded for using an LLM (p. 5). Their contents are unverified; participant-flow documentation or author confirmation is needed rather than assuming that preregistered targets are randomized totals.

Comparison coding is settled as ai_vs_active because the assigned no-LLM condition allowed a browser or search engine (PDF pp. 4-5, 12-13). SI Section 4 is cited for comparisons by actual search-engine use (pp. 9-10), but that use was not described as randomized, so a subgroup comparison must not automatically be recoded as a randomized ai_vs_bau contrast.

Whether the Experiment 4 focal any-stage hypothesis was preregistered remains unverified: the PDF identifies preregistered screenings (p. 13) but calls the result a focal prediction without an explicit preregistration claim (p. 7). S4-O1 remains paper_primary pending the posted preregistration.

Accuracy construct coding is settled as other: these are forecast-accuracy scores, not a named convergent-creativity test. Separately, the four percent-accuracy measure labels remain null because the codebook has no explicit convention for a proportion derived from counts; that mapping needs an internal coding decision and does not determine eligibility.

The ancillary occupation-guessing experiment (S5) requires SI Section 5 to establish its specific assignment, analyzed N, scoring method, analysis unit, AI availability and timing. The brief statement in PDF p. 11 does not establish those details or independent eligibility.

Sample overlap is not stated. Neither separate recruitment descriptions nor use of the same screening criteria establish that participants are disjoint across experiments or papers (PDF pp. 12-13). Author confirmation is needed for sample deduplication; the unchanged reconciliation no-overlap assertion is superseded by the final fields.

The decision rule converting contemporaneous betting odds into accurate versus inaccurate hypotheses is absent from the saved PDF (p. 5, referring to SI Table S1). The specific favored-qualification claim was removed; the supplement or scoring documentation is needed for the exact rule.

Crowd-level unique-team counts, uncertainty and pooling of the factorial cells are not reported in the main text (PDF p. 11, referring to SI Table S21). The supplement is needed for numerical extraction; the existence of the output-based crowd comparison is already explicit.

The Experiment 4 cell grouping used for percent accuracy in Figure 4(b) is not stated (PDF pp. 8-9). The p. 7 pooled total/accurate-count analysis does not establish that grouping; posted analysis data/code would resolve it.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not purely scored on the output: percent confidence (the number of listed teams each participant expects to qualify) and calibration (confidence minus accuracy). LLM users were less confident and underconfident (PDF p. 8; Fig. 4(c)-(d), p. 9; SI Table S5 cited). In Experiment 3, 385 of 395 LLM-condition participants pasted valid raw Perplexity output, and participant totals and accuracy correlated with those of the LLM output (r = .334 and r = .795, p. 10, Fig. 5). The average LLM user performed between the 60th and 81st percentiles of no-LLM performance (p. 11, SI Table S12 cited). The paper states the size of the LLM effect three ways: 'on average 36% more' (abstract, p. 2), '18% to 55%' (significance statement, p. 2) and 'from 30% to 58%' (summary of findings, p. 4); these source discrepancies are not harmonized. Experiment 4 prints '35.20 female' with no percent sign (p. 13). No-LLM arms are coded other_aid because a browser or search engine was allowed; self-reported LLM users in no-LLM conditions were excluded after assignment under preregistered rules. The three additional S4-O1 contrasts retain printed cell means from p. 7 and the significance brackets in Fig. 3, p. 8; these were checked against the PDF. Figure 4 dot positions are not used to supply unprinted numerical values or to assert unspecified cell groupings. Finalization read all 240 markdown lines, extracted text from all 17 PDF pages, and inspected the relevant figure and mathematical notation in memory. No SI Appendix is appended or embedded; local filename searches found no matching supplement, and urllib requests to the named OSF API, OSF project and alternate SSRN source all failed with WinError 10013. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as required. Its unsupported no-overlap assertion and its figure-derived Experiment 4 grouping are superseded by sample_overlap, the updated outcome fields and the final object. The eight challenge resolutions count corrections to unsupported assertions; null fields and separately listed open items do not imply that the challenged assertions were confirmed. Unknown S5 fields use null where the current specification supplies no not_stated option. Core remains unclear because of scope and the unassessable ancillary experiment, despite confirmed random assignment and analyzed sample sizes in the four main experiments.

challenge_resolution.problem: S5-O1; scored_on_output; measure; question; ai_available_when_produced; timing: The ancillary experiment has only a brief task description and a directional result in this PDF. These support the occupation-guessing hypothesis-count outcome and its reported direction, but do not explicitly describe how the count was obtained, whether it was scored from submitted outputs, or whether AI was available during the scored generation rather than at another stage. Immediate timing is also unstated. These method and timing fields remain unverified without SI Section 5; null is preferable to asserting them as confirmed. The existing not_stated unit is appropriately cautious.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Set S5-O1.scored_on_output, measure, question, ai_available_when_produced and timing to null; retained the hypothesis-count outcome and reported higher direction. Also replaced unsupported not_stated enum values with null for its unknown unit and S5 assignment unit/structure, population and AI role. The unavailable SI Section 5 is needed for the experiment-specific methods and eligibility.
challenge_resolution.quote: participants guessed the (single) occupation of a person after reading a brief profile description. Again, using LLMs increased the number of hypotheses that participants generated.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 11, Discussion, ancillary experiment paragraph; SI Appendix Section 5 cited but absent.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-S5; reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked[18] (sample_overlap.shares_participants_with): The saved document describes recruitment for each experiment but never establishes that their participants are disjoint or that none also appear in another paper. In particular, separate Prolific recruitment for S1 and S3 and separate MTurk recruitment for S2 and S4 do not rule out repeat participants. The quoted passage describes S3 recruitment and reuse of screening criteria, not absence of participant overlap. The primary sample_overlap fields are blank, but this reconciliation entry incorrectly treats no overlap as confirmed; overlap remains unknown.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Set the active sample_overlap field to not_stated and added an author-clarification item. Recruitment and repeated screening criteria do not establish absence of overlap. The reconciliation object, including agreed_fields_checked[18], remains unchanged as instructed; this final resolution explicitly supersedes that unsupported no-overlap claim.
challenge_resolution.quote: We used the same preregistered exclusion criteria as in Experiment 1.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 13, Materials and Methods, Experiment 3; recruitment descriptions pp. 12-13 and complete saved PDF contain no explicit statement of disjoint participants.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-S4; open_questions[3]; source.supplement.holds (Table S2); eligibility.reason; studies[].participants.exclusions (claims about per-arm counts in the SI): The PDF says Table S2 summarizes numbers preregistered, dropout rates, and final sample sizes across experiments. It does not establish that the table contains actual randomized counts or counts for each arm; preregistered targets are not randomized totals. The SI Appendix is neither included nor embedded in the 17-page PDF, and no matching local supplement was found. Requests to the cited OSF project, its API, and the alternate SSRN source failed with WinError 10013 (network access blocked), so the claimed table contents could not be checked. The null randomized and individual-arm counts are appropriate, but claims that the unavailable table definitely supplies them are unsupported.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Rewrote source.supplement.holds, all four participant-exclusion notes, eligibility.reason and the participant-count open question. Table S2 is now attributed only numbers preregistered, dropout rates and final sample sizes, as described by the PDF. Claims that it definitely supplies actual randomized or per-arm counts were removed. All unreported randomized and individual-arm count fields remain null.
challenge_resolution.quote: Please see SI Appendix, Table S2 for a summary of number of participants preregistered, dropout rates, and final sample sizes obtained across experiments.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 12, Materials and Methods, opening paragraph; p. 5, Paradigm, Table S4 citation. Neither appendix table was available.

open_items.item: Open question 1: whether the finite-answer playoff-forecast task and its crowd-level breadth qualify under the creativity/ideation scope affects criterion 3. PDF pp. 4-5 and 11 already establish the task and output measures; an internal Review 1 scope decision is needed, with no additional document required.

Open question 2: the Experiment 3 cells actually plotted in Figure 4 conflict with its stated exclusion of incentivized conditions (PDF p. 9 versus p. 6). Posted analysis data/code would establish grouping; this concerns extraction, not the three eligibility criteria.

Open question 3 and reconciliation.differences[9] residual issue: why the abstract reports 1,814 while the four analyzed study counts sum to 1,812 (PDF pp. 2, 12-13). Author clarification would settle the discrepancy; every explicitly reported study N exceeds 50.

Open question 4: exact randomized totals, exclusions and individual-arm analyzed counts need participant-flow documentation or author confirmation. The PDF does not establish that SI Table S2 contains them (p. 12); the stated analyzed totals already meet criterion 2.

Open question 5 is settled for coding: the randomized no-LLM condition permitted search tools, so ai_vs_active stands (PDF pp. 4-5, 12-13). The SI comparison by actual search-engine use does not establish randomized assignment to no aid; no further source is needed for this decision.

Open question 6 and reconciliation.differences[2] residual issue: whether Experiment 4 preregistered the focal any-stage hypothesis, beyond its screenings (PDF pp. 7, 13). The posted OSF preregistration would settle primary-outcome status; preregistration is not an eligibility requirement.

Open question 7 is settled for construct coding as other because these are forecast-accuracy outcomes. A separate internal measure convention is still needed for count-derived accuracy proportions; the four measure values are null. The source formula is explicit (PDF p. 8), and additional paper material is unnecessary for that codebook decision.

Open question 8 and reconciliation.differences[3] residual issue: S5-specific assignment, analyzed people count, output scoring, AI availability and timing are not supplied in PDF p. 11. SI Section 5 is needed to assess all three criteria for this ancillary study and whether it can independently establish paper eligibility.

Open question 9 / people challenge: participant overlap across experiments or papers is not stated (PDF pp. 12-13). Authors must confirm it for sample deduplication; the separate main-study analyzed counts independently exceed 50.

Open question 10 / outcome challenge: the exact betting-odds classification rule is absent (PDF p. 5). SI Table S1 and its scoring details should be inspected; the missing rule affects accuracy extraction, while the existence of output scoring is explicit.

Open question 11: crowd-level counts, uncertainty and pooling of factorial cells require SI Table S21 (PDF p. 11). Their absence prevents numerical extraction but does not obscure that the paper compares unique hypotheses across the outputs participants produced.

Open question 12: Experiment 4 cell grouping for Figure 4(b) percent accuracy is unspecified (PDF pp. 8-9). Posted analysis data/code would settle it; the grouping is no longer asserted from neighbouring count plots.
